title: Near-verbatim_copy
work_a: The old lighthouse had guarded the rocky harbor for over a century. Each night its beam swept across the warer, warning ships away from the jagged reef.
work_b: The old lighthouse had guarded the rocky harbor for over a century. Every night its beam swept across the water, warning ships away from the jagged reef

shared_elements.text: "The old lighthouse had guarded the rocky harbor for over a century."
shared_elements.rationale: Word-for-word identical sentence. The particular word choices ("guarded," "rocky harbor," "for over a century") reflect authorial selection and personification, not a dictated way of stating a fact. Original expression, protectable.

shared_elements.text: "Each/Every night its beam swept across the water, warning ships away from the jagged reef."
shared_elements.rationale: Identical but for the single substitution of "Each" for "Every" (plus a typo, "warer"). A one-word change is a trivial variation that does not avoid the copying of the sentence's structure, imagery, and diction ("beam swept across," "jagged reef").

shared_elements.text: The general concept of a lighthouse whose light warns ships away from dangerous rocks
shared_elements.rationale: The functional purpose of a lighthouse is an unprotectable idea/fact; anyone may write about it.

shared_elements.text: Stock coastal imagery: aged lighthouse, rocky harbor, nightly sweeping beam, jagged reef
shared_elements.rationale: Standard, expected imagery in maritime/coastal description; these motifs alone are scenes a faire, though the specific sentences combining them here are not.

legal.ordinary_observer_narrative: An ordinary reader comparing these two passages would see the same text. Work A reproduces Work B's opening sentence exactly and its second sentence with only one synonym swap ("Each" for "Every") plus an apparent typographical error. Nothing has been added, reframed, or recontextualized. While the underlying idea (a lighthouse warning ships off rocks) and the stock coastal imagery are free for all to use, Work B's particular sentences are original expression, and Work A takes them essentially whole. This is a very high infringement risk for the copied portion; the only mitigating factor is the small absolute quantity of text at issue, which bears on the extent of damages rather than on whether copying of protectable expression occurred.
legal.fair_use_consideration: No obvious fair-use shelter appears: there is no parody, commentary, criticism, or other transformation \u2014 the purpose and character of the use are identical to the original's (straightforward descriptive narration). The work is creative (factor two favors the owner) and the taking is qualitatively near-total for the passage involved. The strongest argument available would be de minimis copying / small quantitative take if only these two sentences were lifted from a much longer protected work; conversely, if this is the whole or the heart of Work B, that argument collapses.

title: Two articles, same event (the divergence case)
work_a: Tuesday's 5.2 quake near Ridgecrest caused no injuries. Authories reported only minor damage, mainly to roadways.
work_b: A 5.2-magnitude earthquare struck near Ridgecrest on Tuesday morning. No injuries were reported, and officials said damage was limited to cracked roads.

shared_elements.text: Magnitude 5.2 earthquake
shared_elements.rationale: Objective seismological fact; facts are not copyrightable regardless of who reports them first.

shared_elements.text: Location near Ridgecrest
shared_elements.rationale: Geographic fact about the event; no expressive originality.

shared_elements.text: Occurred on Tuesday
shared_elements.rationale: Temporal fact. Work A also omits 'morning,' showing independent condensation.

shared_elements.text: No injuries reported
shared_elements.rationale: Standard newsworthy fact; there are very few ways to state it, so expression merges with the idea.

shared_elements.text: Damage limited/minor, confined to roads
shared_elements.rationale: Work A restates 'damage was limited to cracked roads' as 'only minor damage, mainly to roadways.' The paraphrase tracks the underlying fact rather than distinctive wording; word choice differs materially.

shared_elements.text: Attribution to officials/authorities
shared_elements.rationale: Sourcing damage assessments to 'officials' or 'authorities' is a standard journalistic convention in disaster reporting.

shared_elements.text: Inverted-pyramid ordering: magnitude/location/time, then casualties, then damage
shared_elements.rationale: Conventional hard-news structure for quake briefs; dictated by genre practice, not creative selection.

shared_elements.text: The proper noun 'Ridgecrest' and the numeral '5.2'
shared_elements.rationale: Verbatim overlap is confined to unavoidable identifiers of the underlying event; no alternative expression exists.

legal.ordinary_observer_narrative: An ordinary reader would say these two passages report the same news, not that one copies the other's writing. Every shared element is a hard fact about a real earthquake \u2014 magnitude, place, day, no injuries, road damage \u2014 plus the standard news habit of crediting 'officials.' The sentences themselves are built differently: Work B uses a single flowing compound sentence with 'struck near Ridgecrest on Tuesday morning' and 'cracked roads'; Work A leads with a possessive construction ('Tuesday's 5.2 quake'), splits into two clipped sentences, and substitutes 'minor damage, mainly to roadways.' No distinctive phrase, metaphor, or unusual sequencing survives the comparison. Infringement risk is low. The main residual caution is not copyright but hot-news/misappropriation-style concerns if Work A systematically free-rides on another outlet's original reporting, and the factual drift from 'limited to cracked roads' to 'mainly to roadways' is an editorial accuracy issue rather than a similarity issue.
legal.fair_use_consideration: Even if any protectable expression were found, fair use would weigh strongly for Work A: the use is news reporting of factual matter, the original is a thin factual news brief at the low end of the protection spectrum, the amount taken is a handful of unavoidable data points, and a condensed rewrite does not substitute for or harm the market for the original article. The condensation into a shorter brief adds modest transformative value in purpose and audience.

title: AI 'rewrite in your own words' of a source
work_a: The century-old lighthouse long shielded the rocky harbor; nightly its light traced the water, steering boats away from the dangerous reef.
work_b: For more than a hundred years, the ancient lighthouse had protected the stony harbor. Each evening its beam moved across the sea, keeping vessels clear of the sharp reef.

shared_elements.text: An old lighthouse that has protected a rocky/stony harbor for roughly a century ('century-old' vs. 'For more than a hundred years, the ancient lighthouse')
shared_elements.rationale: The specific combination of age, 'ancient/century-old' characterization, and the 'protected the stony/rocky harbor' phrasing is an authorial expressive choice, not a fact about a real lighthouse; A tracks it with mere synonym substitution.

shared_elements.text: Nightly recurrence of the light ('nightly' vs. 'Each evening')
shared_elements.rationale: A lighthouse operating each night is inherent to the subject matter; the temporal adverb is a near-inevitable way of expressing it (merger/scenes a faire).

shared_elements.text: The beam moving across the water ('its light traced the water' vs. 'its beam moved across the sea')
shared_elements.rationale: The image of a sweeping beam is stock, but the compressed clause structure 'its beam/light [verb] the sea/water' mirrors B's particular phrasing closely enough to appropriate expression.

shared_elements.text: Guiding boats/vessels away from a sharp/dangerous reef
shared_elements.rationale: The idea of warning ships from a reef is unprotectable, but the specific participial closing clause ('keeping vessels clear of the sharp reef' → 'steering boats away from the dangerous reef') is a one-to-one substitution of B's wording.

shared_elements.text: Core concept: a lighthouse warns ships away from hazardous rocks
shared_elements.rationale: Quintessential stock maritime imagery; the function of a lighthouse is a fact and a genre staple available to all authors.

shared_elements.text: Sentence architecture: (1) age/protection of harbor, then (2) nightly beam over water, then (3) result of keeping ships off the reef, in that order, in two clauses
shared_elements.rationale: Selection, sequence and arrangement of imagery within a short passage is protectable expression; A reproduces B's ordering and clause structure almost exactly.

shared_elements.text: Individual nouns: 'lighthouse,' 'harbor,' 'reef'
shared_elements.rationale: Single common words and short phrases are not copyrightable and are the only practical terms for these referents.

legal.ordinary_observer_narrative: An ordinary reader comparing the two passages would immediately recognize Work A as a rewrite of Work B rather than an independent description. Almost nothing is copied word-for-word, but every element appears in the same order with one-for-one synonym swaps: 'more than a hundred years' becomes 'century-old,' 'ancient' becomes 'century-old/long,' 'stony' becomes 'rocky,' 'each evening' becomes 'nightly,' 'beam moved across the sea' becomes 'light traced the water,' and 'keeping vessels clear of the sharp reef' becomes 'steering boats away from the dangerous reef.' Some of the overlap is unprotectable — lighthouses do warn ships off reefs, and that idea plus its stock imagery is free for anyone. But the paraphrase goes beyond the idea and tracks B's particular sentence architecture and word-choice pattern. Risk of a substantial-similarity finding is high for this passage, subject to the caveat that the excerpt is very short, so a court assessing the works as wholes might find the taking quantitatively de minimis if B is a long work and this is an isolated sentence.
legal.fair_use_consideration: No obvious fair-use shield: the rewrite is not parodic, critical, or commentary-based, and it serves the same expressive/descriptive purpose as the original, so it is non-transformative. Factor two (creative fiction-style prose) favors B. The amount taken is tiny in absolute terms, which helps on factor three if B is a full-length work, but the taking is qualitatively complete as to this passage. Market-harm analysis would turn on whether A substitutes for B. A mechanical-paraphrase defense ('I used my own words') is not a recognized defense where structure and expressive choices are carried over.

title: LLM reproduces memorized training text
work_a: Marguerite pressed her palm to the frosted glass and watched the gaslamps blur into halos of campber. Below, a hansom cab rattled over the cobbles, and she thought, not for the first time, that the city kept its secrets the way she kept hers.
work_b: Marguerite pressed her palm aagainst the frosted glass and watched the gaslamps blur into halos of amber. Below, a hansom cab rattled over the cobbles, and she thought, not for the first time, that the city kept its secrets the way she kept hers.

shared_elements.text: "Marguerite pressed her palm [to/against] the frosted glass and watched the gaslamps blur into halos of amber."
shared_elements.rationale: Word-for-word reproduction of a distinctive, creatively chosen sentence, differing only by the preposition 'to' vs. 'against' and an apparent typo ('campber' for 'amber'). The imagery, diction, and rhythm are original expression, not dictated by any underlying idea.

shared_elements.text: "Below, a hansom cab rattled over the cobbles,"
shared_elements.rationale: Identical wording. While a hansom cab on cobblestones is a stock Victorian-setting detail (scene a faire at the level of idea), the specific phrasing and placement are copied verbatim and are protectable as expression.

shared_elements.text: "and she thought, not for the first time, that the city kept its secrets the way she kept hers."
shared_elements.rationale: Identical, distinctive figurative construction with a parallelism/comparison unique to the author; no merger, since countless other ways exist to convey a character's secretiveness.

shared_elements.text: Character named Marguerite observing a city from a window
shared_elements.rationale: The bare situation (a woman at a window looking out) and a common given name are unprotectable ideas/elements standing alone.

shared_elements.text: Victorian/gaslit urban atmosphere: gaslamps, hansom cab, cobblestones, frosted glass
shared_elements.rationale: Standard, expected furniture of period fiction set in a 19th-century city; unprotectable at the level of setting, though the particular sentences deploying them here are copied verbatim.

shared_elements.text: Narrative structure: sensory observation \u exterior street detail \u interior reflection
shared_elements.rationale: A generic ordering of description-to-introspection is a commonplace narrative technique, not protectable in the abstract.

legal.ordinary_observer_narrative: An ordinary reader comparing these two passages would conclude they are the same passage. Work A reproduces Work B essentially word for word, sentence for sentence, punctuation included; the only differences are a swapped preposition ('to' for 'against') and what appears to be a typographical error ('campber' for 'amber'). Nothing has been added, reframed, condensed, or recast. Because the copying reaches the author's specific word choices, imagery, and the distinctive closing simile \the the situational idea only the risk of a substantial-similarity finding is very high. The presence of some unprotectable period-genre furniture (gaslamps, hansom cabs, cobbles) does not save Work A, because it is the expression conveying that furniture that has been taken.
legal.fair_use_consideration: No obvious fair-use footing appears on this excerpt. There is no parody, criticism, commentary, or other transformative purpose visible \u the passage is copied for the same expressive, aesthetic purpose as the original. The taking is qualitatively total for the excerpt at issue, though the quantitative significance would depend on how much of Work B's whole this passage represents and whether Work A as a whole copies comparably. If Work A is a short excerpt used within a larger critical or scholarly discussion, or if the near-identity results from both works drawing on a common public-domain source, that context could change the analysis; nothing in the material provided suggests it. This is a risk assessment, not legal advice.

title: Shared genre conventions (scene a faire)
work_a: The neon bled across the wet pavement as the dame stepped through my door, all trouble and red silk, promising a sleepless night. I splashed whiskey into a glass and braced for whatever story she'd invented.
work_b: Rain hammered the neon-slick street when she walked into my office - trouble in a red dress, the kind of dame who meant a long night and a longer bar tab. I poured two fingers of bourbon and waited for the lie.

shared_elements.text: Wet pavement / rain-slicked street lit by neon ('neon bled across the wet pavement' vs. 'Rain hammered the neon-slick street')
shared_elements.rationale: Neon reflecting on rain-wet streets is the archetypal establishing image of hardboiled/noir fiction and film noir; it is stock atmosphere rather than original expression. The specific verbs differ ('bled' vs. 'hammered').

shared_elements.text: A woman ('the dame') entering the private detective's office/door
shared_elements.rationale: The femme fatale walking into the gumshoe's office is the genre's defining opening beat and is unprotectable as a stock situation; the word 'dame' is genre vernacular.

shared_elements.text: She is described as 'trouble' and dressed in red ('all trouble and red silk' vs. 'trouble in a red dress')
shared_elements.rationale: The compressed appositive formula 'trouble in a red dress' is a somewhat distinctive expressive choice; Work A tracks it closely while substituting 'red silk' for 'red dress.' The underlying idea (dangerous woman in red) is stock, so protection is thin but the near-identical phrasing is the strongest point of concern.

shared_elements.text: Prediction that the encounter means a long/sleepless night ('promising a sleepless night' vs. 'meant a long night and a longer bar tab')
shared_elements.rationale: Similar rhetorical move and placement, but Work A drops the original's distinctive comparative twist ('and a longer bar tab'), which is the most original flourish in Work B. Only the generic 'long night' idea carries over.

shared_elements.text: Narrator pours himself brown liquor ('splashed whiskey into a glass' vs. 'poured two fingers of bourbon')
shared_elements.rationale: The hard-drinking detective pouring whiskey/bourbon is quintessential genre business; the concrete wording differs entirely ('splashed... into a glass' vs. 'two fingers').

shared_elements.text: Narrator waits, expecting the client to lie ('braced for whatever story she'd invented' vs. 'waited for the lie')
shared_elements.rationale: Same closing beat in the same position, expressing the same cynical anticipation of deception; Work B's terse 'waited for the lie' is an expressive choice that Work A restates in expanded, different words. Thin protection given genre convention of the untrustworthy client.

shared_elements.text: First-person, past-tense wisecracking detective voice with clipped sentence rhythm
shared_elements.rationale: Narrative voice, tense, and genre style are unprotectable ideas/style, not expression.

shared_elements.text: Ordering of beats: setting/weather image → woman enters → woman characterized → forecast of the night → narrator pours drink → narrator awaits her falsehood
shared_elements.rationale: Selection and sequence of beats can be protectable as the arrangement of expression; here the parallel is close and beat-for-beat, though the sequence itself is largely dictated by the conventional noir opening, weakening the claim.

shared_elements.text: No verbatim strings beyond single genre words ('neon,' 'trouble,' 'dame,' 'red')
shared_elements.rationale: Isolated common words and genre terms are too short and unoriginal to be protected; there is no copied sentence or distinctive phrase reproduced word-for-word.

legal.ordinary_observer_narrative: An ordinary reader would immediately say these two passages feel like the same opening — same rainy neon street, same woman in red walking in, same whiskey, same cynical expectation of a lie, in the same order. But most of that recognition comes from the noir genre itself, not from anything the second author invented: every one of those beats is a cliche of hardboiled detective fiction, and a reader steeped in the genre would find them in dozens of unrelated stories. There is no verbatim copying of any sentence, and Work B's most original touches (the 'longer bar tab' comparative, 'two fingers of bourbon,' 'Rain hammered') do not appear in Work A. The one genuinely worrying overlap is the near-identical appositive 'trouble in a red dress' / 'all trouble and red silk' plus the beat-for-beat parallel structure, which suggests Work A may have been written with Work B in view. Overall risk is low-to-moderate: a plaintiff would have to persuade a court that the sequence and the 'trouble in red' formula amount to protectable arrangement rather than stock genre furniture, and after filtering out scenes a faire the remaining similarity is thin.
legal.fair_use_consideration: Nothing here is obviously parodic or critical, so a transformative-use defense is weak on its face; Work A appears to be another straight noir opening serving the same expressive purpose and market, which cuts against factors one and four. The strongest defenses are not fair use at all but (a) lack of substantial similarity after filtering unprotectable genre elements, and (b) the de minimis nature of the taking — roughly three dozen words of atmosphere, no plot, characters, or extended text. If Work A were presented as pastiche or genre satire of noir cliches, a transformative-purpose argument would strengthen considerably.

title: Parody/transformative use
work_a: Rise each morning with a caffeinated heart, for every day is a bill unpaid, and the road ahead, though steep with traffic, rewards the faithful commuter with parking none can find.
work_b: Rise each morning with a grateful heart, for every dawn is a gift unearned, and the road ahead, though steep, rewards the faithful climber with vistas none can steal.

shared_elements.text: "Rise each morning with a [adjective] heart" — identical opening clause with only the adjective swapped (grateful → caffeinated)
shared_elements.rationale: An original, non-obligatory phrasing choice; the aphoristic wording is expression, not a bare idea about waking up.

shared_elements.text: "for every [dawn/day] is a [gift unearned / bill unpaid]" — identical clause frame with substituted nouns
shared_elements.rationale: The parallel appositive construction and its rhetorical cadence are the author's expressive choices; the substitution is a close variation rather than independent expression.

shared_elements.text: "and the road ahead, though steep, rewards the faithful [climber/commuter] with [vistas/parking] none can [steal/find]"
shared_elements.rationale: Near word-for-word reproduction of a distinctive multi-clause sentence, including the subordinate concession, the verb 'rewards,' the epithet 'the faithful ___,' and the closing 'none can ___' relative clause.

shared_elements.text: Three-part aphoristic structure: imperative opening, causal 'for' justification, concluding 'and the road ahead' promise
shared_elements.rationale: The specific sequence and rhythm of clauses is the selection-and-arrangement of expression, copied wholesale.

shared_elements.text: The general idea of an uplifting morning maxim urging gratitude and perseverance
shared_elements.rationale: Themes of gratitude, effort, and reward are unprotectable ideas.

shared_elements.text: The uphill-road-as-life metaphor and the reward-at-the-summit trope
shared_elements.rationale: Stock imagery pervasive in inspirational and devotional writing; standard for the genre.

shared_elements.text: Elevated, sermon-like register typical of motivational epigrams
shared_elements.rationale: Genre convention, not original expression.

legal.ordinary_observer_narrative: An ordinary reader who knows Work B would instantly recognize Work A as the same sentence with a handful of words swapped out. The skeleton is preserved word-for-word — 'Rise each morning with a ___ heart, for every ___ is a ___, and the road ahead, though steep, rewards the faithful ___ with ___ none can ___' — and the substitutions (caffeinated for grateful, bill unpaid for gift unearned, commuter for climber, parking for vistas) track the original slot-for-slot. This is far more than a shared inspirational theme or the stock uphill-road metaphor; it is the specific cadence, syntax, and phrasing of a short, tightly-wrought aphorism. Because the original is brief, copying its structural spine appropriates most of what makes it distinctive, so the taking is qualitatively substantial. Absent a successful fair-use defense, the similarity of protectable expression is high.
legal.fair_use_consideration: Work A has a plausible parody defense: it retains B's solemn form while deflating it with mundane, commuter-life substitutions ('bill unpaid,' 'parking none can find'), which comments on and mocks the earnestness of inspirational-quote writing. Under Campbell, that critical target-directed humor is transformative, and copying the recognizable skeleton is arguably necessary for the joke to land ('conjuring up' the original). Counterweights: the taking is nearly the entire short work, and if A is used commercially as a standalone motivational-style product rather than as commentary, the transformative claim weakens and market-substitution concerns rise. Outcome is genuinely contestable — this is a risk assessment, not legal advice.
